nasa_sealevel/gmsl_vital_sign.csv.retrieval_method: NASA/NOAA/NSIDC endpoint fetched in a real browser on 2026-11-05; SHA-256 of the stored file verified equal to the SHA-256 computed in the browser on the bytes received

parameters.name: Global mean surface temperature anomaly
limitations: El Niño/La Niña (ENSO) is not modelled explicitly; it shifts global temperature by roughly ±0.1-0.2 °C from year to year, which dominates a two-year outlook.
GISTEMP values are revised slightly every month as late station and ship reports arrive.
The October 2026 value had not been published at retrieval (GISTEMP releases mid-month).
parameters.description: The global average of near-surface air temperature over land and sea-surface temperature over the ocean, expressed as a departure from the 1951–1980 average. It is the primary indicator of global warming.

source.agency: NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS)
source.citation: GISTEMP Team, 2026: GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP), version 4. NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies. Lenssen et al. (2024), JGR Atmospheres.
source.spatial_coverage: Global (land stations GHCNv4 + ocean ERSSTv5), 2x2 degree grid aggregated to a global mean
source.typical_delay: Published around the 10th-20th of the following month; the October 2026 value was not yet released at retrieval.

naive.label: Persistence (naive)
naive.description: Every future month equals the last observed month.

snaive.label: Seasonal naive
snaive.description: Each future month equals the same calendar month one year earlier (repeated).

drift.label: Random walk with drift
drift.description: Last value plus the average month-to-month change over the last 30 years (seasonal: year-on-year change, applied to the last year).

linear.label: Linear regression (trend + month effects)
linear.description: Ordinary least squares on a linear time trend (plus calendar-month dummies for seasonal series), fitted to the most recent 30 years.

poly2.label: Polynomial regression (quadratic)
poly2.description: Quadratic time trend (captures acceleration) plus calendar-month dummies, fitted to the most recent 30 years.

ets.label: Exponential smoothing (Holt-Winters, damped)
ets.description: Additive-error exponential smoothing with a damped additive trend and additive seasonality where the series is seasonal (statsmodels).

sarima.label: ARIMA / SARIMA
sarima.description: Seasonal ARIMA with order chosen by AIC from a small candidate set on the full training record, then re-estimated at every validation origin (statsmodels SARIMAX).

gbr.label: Gradient boosting (lag features)
gbr.description: scikit-learn GradientBoostingRegressor predicting the month-to-month change from lagged changes, lagged levels relative to the 12-month mean and calendar month; multi-step forecasts are produced recursively. Trees cannot extrapolate levels, so the model works on differences.

not_used.prophet: Not used: Prophet's piecewise-linear trend with automatic changepoints adds a heavy dependency and, for these smooth monthly climate series, offers nothing beyond the ETS/SARIMA/regression trend models already validated here.
not_used.lstm: Not used: each series has 300-1,800 monthly points (a few hundred independent seasonal cycles). That is far too little to train a recurrent network without overfitting, and deep models cannot be justified over the statistical models on out-of-sample skill at this sample size.

modelling.interval_method: Gaussian intervals scaled by the selected model's horizon-specific out-of-sample RMSE (made non-decreasing with horizon).

interval_coverage_check.note: In-sample to the validation folds (the same errors set the interval width), so this checks calibration shape rather than giving an independent test.

residuals.interpretation: no significant autocorrelation left in one-step errors (Ljung-Box p > 0.05); systematic bias of -0.029 per month (t-test p <= 0.05); errors consistent with normality.

parameters.name: Atmospheric CO₂ concentration (Mauna Loa)
limitations: Single-station record; recent months are provisional and can be revised by NOAA by a few tenths of a ppm.
The forecast extrapolates the recent growth rate; it assumes no abrupt change in global emissions or land/ocean uptake.
parameters.description: The monthly mean concentration of carbon dioxide in dry air at Mauna Loa Observatory, Hawaii — the longest continuous direct record of atmospheric CO₂. A seasonal cycle driven by Northern Hemisphere plant growth sits on top of a steady rise.

source.agency: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory (record shown on NASA's Climate Vital Signs)
source.dataset: Mauna Loa Observatory monthly mean CO2 (co2_mm_mlo)
source.citation: Lan, X., Tans, P. and Thoning, K.W.: Trends in globally-averaged CO2 determined from NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory measurements. NOAA GML.
source.spatial_coverage: Single station (Mauna Loa, Hawaii, 19.5N 155.6W); representative of the well-mixed background atmosphere
source.typical_delay: Monthly file regenerated in the first days of the following month (file creation 9 Oct 2026 contained September 2026).
source.notes: NASA does not operate the long-term in-situ CO2 record; NASA's Vital Signs page displays this NOAA series. Values were cross-checked: all 823 monthly means in the stored file are identical to NOAA's live file (canonical SHA-256 match).

parameters.name: Global sea surface temperature anomaly
limitations: ERSSTv5 is a NOAA reconstruction (the ocean input to NASA GISTEMP); NASA satellite SST products need an Earthdata login.
ENSO phase changes dominate year-to-year global ocean temperature and are not predicted explicitly.
parameters.description: The average temperature of the ocean's surface layer over the global ocean, as a departure from the 1901–2000 average. The ocean absorbs most of the excess heat in the climate system, and this record also carries the signature of El Niño and La Niña.

source.agency: NOAA NCEI (ERSSTv5 - the ocean component used inside NASA GISTEMP)
source.dataset: Climate at a Glance: Global Ocean surface temperature anomalies (ERSSTv5-based)
source.citation: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, Climate at a Glance: Global Time Series (2026).
source.spatial_coverage: Global ocean, 2x2 degree ERSSTv5 grid aggregated to a global ocean mean
source.typical_delay: Released around the 12th-15th of the following month.
source.notes: NASA's satellite SST products (e.g. MUR via PO.DAAC) require an Earthdata login. ERSSTv5 is the sea-surface temperature input that NASA GISTEMP itself uses, so this series is consistent with the GISTEMP global index.

parameters.name: Global mean sea level
limitations: The most recent calendar month is built from fewer weekly samples than usual (partial month).
The annual cycle is retained in the NASA series, so month-to-month changes include seasonal water exchange between land and ocean.
parameters.description: The average height of the global ocean surface measured by satellite radar altimeters since 1993, relative to a reference level near the start of the record. It rises as sea water warms and expands and as glaciers and ice sheets add water; the annual cycle is kept.

source.dataset: Global Mean Sea Level vital sign (satellite altimetry: TOPEX/Poseidon, Jason-1/2/3, Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich)
source.citation: NASA Sea Level Change Portal, Global Mean Sea Level; underlying dataset NASA_SSH_GMSL_INDICATOR (PO.DAAC).
source.temporal_resolution: About 7 days (aggregated here to calendar-month means)
source.baseline: Height relative to the 1993-2008 reference (series starts near 0 in 1993); annual cycle retained
source.typical_delay: Near-real-time; the series extended to decimal year 2026.82 (late October 2026) at retrieval.
source.notes: Extracted from the data array embedded in the NASA vital-sign page. The same series is distributed as NASA_SSH_GMSL_INDICATOR.txt on PO.DAAC (Earthdata login required); the pipeline uses that file instead when EARTHDATA_TOKEN is configured.

parameters.name: Arctic sea ice extent
limitations: December 1987 and January 1988 are missing (satellite gap) and interpolated only for model fitting.
Summer extent is strongly controlled by weather in a given year, so single-year forecasts carry wide uncertainty even though the long-term decline is clear.
parameters.description: The area of the Arctic Ocean with at least 15% sea-ice cover, observed by passive-microwave satellites since late 1978. Extent peaks in March and reaches its minimum in September; summer ice is a sensitive indicator of Arctic warming.

source.agency: NSIDC (NASA DAAC) - Sea Ice Index, version 4
source.dataset: Sea Ice Index G02135 v4.0 - Northern Hemisphere monthly extent
source.citation: Fetterer, F., K. Knowles, W. N. Meier, M. Savoie, and A. K. Windnagel. Sea Ice Index, Version 4. NSIDC.
source.temporal_resolution: Monthly (derived from daily passive-microwave data: NASA SMMR, DMSP SSM/I-SSMIS)
source.spatial_coverage: Northern Hemisphere (Arctic), 25 km polar stereographic grid
source.typical_delay: Monthly files refreshed within the first days of the next month (files dated 2 Nov 2026 include October 2026).
source.notes: December 1987 and January 1988 are missing in the source (satellite data gap); they are linearly interpolated for modelling only and flagged as estimated.

parameters.name: Precipitation (global grid-sample index)
limitations: This is a 126-point sample index (60°S-60°N) from MERRA-2-based POWER data, not a gridded global precipitation product such as GPCP or IMERG.

The latest months in POWER can come from a near-real-time stream and may be revised; the last 12 months are unusually wet in this index, so a projected decrease reflects expected return toward normal, not a downward trend.
parameters.description: Bias-corrected total precipitation from NASA's MERRA-2 reanalysis (via POWER), averaged with area weights over a 126-point global sample between 60°S and 60°N. It tracks large-scale changes in the global water cycle.

source.agency: NASA Langley Research Center - POWER project (MERRA-2 reanalysis)
source.dataset: POWER Monthly API v2.10, 126-point global grid sample (20 degree spacing, 60S-60N)
source.citation: NASA Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources (POWER) Project, NASA Langley Research Center; data from NASA GMAO MERRA-2.
source.spatial_coverage: 126 grid points (lat -60..60 by 20, lon -170..170 by 20) combined with cos(latitude) area weights; polar caps not sampled
source.baseline: Absolute values; anomalies computed against 1991-2020 calendar-month climatology
source.typical_delay: Monthly aggregates are published after the month closes; MERRA-2 aerosol fields lag further (AOD available through July 2026 at retrieval).
source.notes: A 126-point sample is an index of large-scale behaviour, not a true global gridded mean. It is suitable for trend direction and anomaly detection; absolute values should not be compared with GPCP/IMERG global means.

parameters.name: Land surface air temperature anomaly
limitations: Near-surface air temperature from land weather stations, not satellite land-surface skin temperature (MODIS LST needs an Earthdata login).
parameters.description: Near-surface air temperature measured at land weather stations worldwide, combined into a global index and expressed as a departure from the 1951–1980 average. Land warms faster than the ocean surface.

source.agency: NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS)
source.citation: GISTEMP Team, 2026: GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP), version 4. NASA GISS.
source.spatial_coverage: Global, land meteorological stations only (GHCNv4), extrapolated up to 1200 km
source.typical_delay: Same release cycle as GISTEMP LOTI (mid following month).
source.notes: This is near-surface AIR temperature over land from weather stations, not satellite land-surface SKIN temperature (MODIS LST). MODIS LST requires an Earthdata login and was not retrievable without credentials; the station index is the closest openly published NASA land-temperature record.

parameters.name: Aerosol optical depth at 550 nm (global grid-sample index)
limitations: Aerosol optical depth comes from the MERRA-2 reanalysis (a model constrained by satellite retrievals), sampled at 126 points; it is not a direct observation.
Episodic events (wildfire seasons, dust outbreaks, volcanic eruptions) drive much of the variability and cannot be predicted from past values; the historical trend is not statistically significant.
Latest available month is July 2026 (MERRA-2 aerosol fields lag the meteorology).
parameters.description: Aerosol optical depth at 550 nm — how strongly airborne particles such as dust, smoke, sea salt and pollution dim sunlight — from MERRA-2 (2001 onward) at the same 126 sample points. Higher values mean hazier air.

source.agency: NASA Langley Research Center - POWER project (MERRA-2 reanalysis)
source.dataset: POWER Monthly API v2.10, 126-point global grid sample (20 degree spacing, 60S-60N)
source.citation: NASA Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources (POWER) Project, NASA Langley Research Center; data from NASA GMAO MERRA-2.

interval_coverage_check.note: In-sample to the validation folds (the same errors set the interval width), so this checks calibration shape rather than giving an independent test.

residuals.interpretation: one-step errors remain autocorrelated (Ljung-Box p <= 0.05): the model misses some persistent structure, so intervals may be optimistic; no significant bias; errors consistent with normality.

correlations.caveat: Correlation is not causation. Annual-mean levels share long-term trends, which inflates level correlations; correlations of year-to-year changes remove the shared trend but are noisier.

gistemp_grid.source: NASA GISTEMP v4 (GHCNv4 + ERSSTv5, 1200 km smoothing), 2x2 degree grid averaged to 10x10 degree blocks (cos-latitude weighted; blocks with fewer than 13 valid 2-degree cells left blank).

power_points.source: NASA POWER monthly point API (MERRA-2), 126 grid points.

insights.title: Very likely to be higher by 2028
insights.text: The validated forecasts give at least a 90% chance that the November 2027 – October 2028 average will exceed the latest 12 months for CO₂ (100.0%) and sea level (99.9%).

insights.title: Likely, but not certain, to be higher
insights.text: Aerosol optical depth (79%), sea surface temperature (76%) and global temperature (70%): more likely than not to rise, with probabilities between 66% and 90%. Year-to-year variability is large enough that a lower two-year average remains possible.

insights.title: Projected to be lower
insights.text: Precipitation (1% chance of an increase) is projected lower: an expected return toward normal after an unusually high recent 12 months, not a long-term decline (its 30-year trend is not statistically significant).

insights.title: No clear direction over two years
insights.text: For Arctic sea ice (59%) and land temperature (48%), the projected change is small compared with year-to-year variability and forecast error. Their long-term records still show: Arctic sea ice decreasing; land temperature increasing. A clear long-term trend can coexist with an uncertain two-year outlook.

insights.title: CO₂ growth is the most predictable signal
insights.text: Mauna Loa CO₂ averaged 428.7 ppm over Oct 2025 – Sep 2026. The selected model (Polynomial regression (quadratic)) projects 434.8 ppm for Nov 2027-Oct 2028 (95% interval +5.1 to +7.0 ppm change). The 30-year trend is 22.4 ppm per decade and the recent 15-year rate is 25.2 ppm per decade versus 19.8 before.

insights.title: Sea-level rise has accelerated
insights.text: Satellite altimetry shows global mean sea level rising 3.6 mm/yr over Nov 2011 – Oct 2026 compared with 2.6 mm/yr over Nov 1996 – Oct 2011. The projected change in the annual mean to Nov 2027-Oct 2028 is +8.9 mm (95% interval +3.5 to +14.3).

insights.title: Global temperature: high level, but year-to-year swings dominate a 2-year outlook
insights.text: GISTEMP's latest monthly anomaly is +1.38 °C (Sep 2026, vs 1951-1980), ranked #2 of 147 for that calendar month. The 30-year trend is +0.25 °C/decade, but over two years ENSO-driven variability (not modelled explicitly) is comparable in size, which is why the interval is wide.

insights.title: Arctic sea ice continues its long decline, with large variability
insights.text: The 30-year trend in monthly extent is -0.51 million km² per decade. September 2026 extent was 4.81 million km²; the three lowest Septembers on record are 2012 (3.57), 2020 (4.00), 2007 (4.27).

insights.title: Where warming is strongest
insights.text: In GISTEMP's 1981-2025 change map the Arctic (64-90°N) warmed 2.94 °C versus 0.93 °C for the globe (about 3.1×). Northern mid-latitudes (24-64°N) warmed 1.46 °C, the tropics 0.71 °C and the Southern Ocean belt (64-24°S) only 0.44 °C.

insights.title: Co-variability (not causation)
insights.text: After removing shared trends (year-to-year differences, 1993-2025), the strongest statistically significant associations are: Global temperature & Land temperature r = +0.94; Global temperature & Sea surface temperature r = +0.84; Sea surface temperature & Land temperature r = +0.67. These reflect shared physical drivers (e.g. ENSO) or measurement overlap and do not by themselves establish cause.

insights.title: What the uncertainty bands mean
insights.text: Intervals come from each model's own errors when it was repeatedly re-trained on past data and asked to forecast the following months (20 rolling origins). They capture typical forecast error, not structural surprises such as a major volcanic eruption, a step change in emissions, or an instrument change.

insights.title: Why these trends matter
insights.text: Rising CO₂ is the dominant driver of the long-term warming seen in the temperature records (an attribution established by physical climate science, not by the correlations computed here). Warmer oceans and melting land ice raise sea level, which compounds coastal flooding; Arctic sea-ice loss reduces surface reflectivity and amplifies regional warming.
